claim: Imprinted X-inactivation silences genes exclusively on the paternally-inherited X-chromosome in mammals.
source: Imprinted X-inactivation silences genes exclusively on the paternally-inherited X-chromosome and is a paradigm of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In maternal-null (Eedm-/-) but not zygotic-null (Eed-/-) early embryos, the maternal X-chromosome ectopically induced Xist and underwent inactivation.
source: In maternal-null (Eedm-/-) but not zygotic-null (Eed-/-) early embryos, the maternal X-chromosome ectopically induced Xist and underwent inactivation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH data presented in Figures 3-7.

claim: Eedm-/- females subsequently stochastically silenced Xist from one of the two X-chromosomes and displayed random X-inactivation.
source: Eedm-/- females subsequently stochastically silenced Xist from one of the two X-chromosomes and displayed random X-inactivation.
evidence: This finding is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data showing mosaic patterns of Xist expression in Eedm-/- blastocysts (Figures 6-7).

claim: The effect of maternal EED loss was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-).
source: This effect was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-), suggesting that zygotic EED can also contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data showing greater paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedmz-/- compared to Eedm-/- embryos (Figure 4).

claim: Zygotic EED can contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
source: This effect was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-), suggesting that zygotic EED can also contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos showing differential effects on X-inactivation.

claim: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos.
source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Xist RNA coating patterns in Eedm-/- mouse embryos with published data on human embryos, and RNA-Seq data showing lack of PRC2 expression in human oocytes (Figure 8).

claim: Human embryos lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2.
source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data from human oocytes showing negligible expression of core PRC2 genes (Figure 8A).

claim: Human embryos only undergo random X-inactivation.
source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the manuscript (Okamoto et al., 2011; Petropoulos et al., 2016).

claim: Expression of PRC2 in the oocyte and transmission of the gene products to the embryo may dictate the occurrence of imprinted X-inactivation in mammals.
source: Thus, expression of PRC2 in the oocyte and transmission of the gene products to the embryo may dictate the occurrence of imprinted X-inactivation in mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparison of mouse and human oocyte PRC2 expression and the phenotypes of maternal EED mutants.

claim: Imprinted X-inactivation results in the silencing of genes exclusively on the paternal X-chromosome and initiates during preimplantation embryogenesis.
source: Imprinted X-inactivation results in the silencing of genes exclusively on the paternal X-chromosome and initiates during preimplantation embryogenesis (Huynh and Lee, 2003; Mak et al., 2004; Monk and Kathuria, 1977; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage.
source: In later stage embryos, imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage (Harper et al., 1982; Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975; West et al., 1977), which subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome (Lyon, 1961).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The embryonic lineage subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome.
source: In later stage embryos, imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage (Harper et al., 1982; Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975; West et al., 1977), which subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome (Lyon, 1961).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Both imprinted and random X-inactivation are prefaced by the expression of X-linked non-protein coding Xist RNA from the prospective inactive-X.
source: Both imprinted and random X-inactivation are prefaced by the expression of X-linked non-protein coding Xist RNA from the prospective inactive-X (Kay et al., 1994; Penny et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During imprinted X-inactivation in the mouse embryo, Xist is expressed at the two-cell stage and the RNA visibly begins to coat the paternal-X at the four-cell stage.
source: During imprinted X-inactivation in the mouse embryo, Xist is expressed at the two-cell stage and the RNA visibly begins to coat the paternal-X at the four-cell stage (Kalantry et al., 2009; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The progressive accumulation of Xist RNA coincides with the gradual and stereotyped silencing of paternal X-linked genes that is only completed after the blastocyst stage of embryogenesis.
source: The progressive accumulation of Xist RNA coincides with the gradual and stereotyped silencing of paternal X-linked genes that is only completed after the blastocyst stage of embryogenesis (Kalantry et al., 2009; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Coincident with Xist RNA coating, Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) proteins and the PRC2-catalyzed chromatin mark histone H3K27me3 accumulate on the inactive-X, correlating with the silencing of X-linked genes.
source: Coincident with Xist RNA coating, Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) proteins and the PRC2-catalyzed chromatin mark histone H3K27me3 accumulate on the inactive-X, correlating with the silencing of X-linked genes (Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3.
source: Moreover, the mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 (de la Cruz et al., 2005; Kohlmaier et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003), suggesting that Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
source: Moreover, the mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 (de la Cruz et al., 2005; Kohlmaier et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003), suggesting that Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations cited in the literature.

claim: PRC2 has been suggested to contribute to the establishment of X-inactivation.
source: PRC2 has thus been suggested to contribute to the establishment of X-inactivation (Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Post-implantation female mouse embryos mutant for the Polycomb gene Eed fail to maintain silencing of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation.
source: Consistent with a role for PRC2 in X-inactivation, we and others previously showed that post-implantation female mouse embryos mutant for the Polycomb gene Eed fail to maintain silencing of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and others, as cited.

claim: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex.
source: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex, but EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2.
source: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex, but EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When EED is mutated other core PRC2 proteins are degraded and the histone H3K27me3 mark is lost.
source: When EED is mutated other core PRC2 proteins are degraded and the histone H3K27me3 mark is lost (Montgomery et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: EED is an essential component of PRC2 and EED function is canonically equated with H3K27me3 catalysis.
source: Thus, EED is an essential component of PRC2 and EED function is canonically equated with H3K27me3 catalysis (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Montgomery et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation.
source: Although Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation, the mutant embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, as cited.

claim: Eed-/- embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly.
source: Although Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation, the mutant embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, as cited.

claim: Eed-/- embryos inherit maternal EED protein that is present in the oocyte.
source: A potential answer for this difference is that Eed-/- embryos inherit maternal EED protein that is present in the oocyte (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Plath et al., 2003; Shumacher et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations and tested in this study.

claim: The presence of maternally-derived EED protein could explain the absence of a defect in establishing imprinted X-inactivation in Eed-/- embryos.
source: The presence of maternally-derived EED protein could explain the absence of a defect in establishing imprinted X-inactivation in Eed-/- embryos.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the study.

claim: Maternal control of imprinted X-inactivation would be consistent with a transgenerational epigenetic effect that underlies genomic imprinting.
source: Such maternal control of imprinted X-inactivation would also be consistent with a transgenerational epigenetic effect that underlies genomic imprinting (Barlow, 2011; Ferguson-Smith and Bourc'his, 2018; Lee and Bartolomei, 2013; van Otterdijk and Michels, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on established concepts of genomic imprinting, supported by citations.

claim: PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 are first enriched on the prospective inactive paternal X-chromosome in the early mouse embryo at the 8–16 cell morula stage.
source: PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 are first enriched on the prospective inactive paternal X-chromosome in the early mouse embryo at the 8–16 cell morula stage (Okamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos are in the process of silencing paternal X-linked genes and establishing imprinted X-inactivation.
source: We assessed the accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA by immunofluorescence (IF) combined with RNA fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) in wild-type (WT) embryonic day (E) 3.5 blastocyst embryos (Cloutier et al., 2018; Hinten et al., 2016), which are in the process of silencing paternal X-linked genes and establishing imprinted X-inactivation (Borensztein et al., 2017; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos, females displayed coincident accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA in a vast majority of the nuclei (72–100%).
source: As expected, females displayed coincident accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA in a vast majority of the nuclei (72–100%).
evidence: This is supported by IF/FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos, males lacked enrichment of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA.
source: Males, by contrast, lacked such enrichment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by IF/FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein.
source: Together, the results in Figure 1 suggest that genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein and that expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
evidence: This is inferred from IF data showing EED and H3K27me3 enrichment in some embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses (Figure 1B).

claim: Expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
source: Together, the results in Figure 1 suggest that genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein and that expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
evidence: This is inferred from IF data showing variable EED and H3K27me3 enrichment patterns in embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses (Figure 1B).

claim: There is no bias in the sex ratio or genotype of embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses.
source: Embryos from 12 litters showed no statistical difference in the distribution of Eed+/- and Eed-/- male or female embryos (p>0.05), suggesting that the intermediate class of 23 embryos in Figure 1A are likely a mixture of Eed+/- or Eed-/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3.
source: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3, whereas Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3 (Figures 2A, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- 2-cell embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3.
source: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3, whereas Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3 (Figures 2A, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 2-cell embryo harbors only maternally-derived EED and H3K27me3.
source: These data are consistent with the 2-cell embryo harboring only maternally-derived EED and H3K27me3.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- 2-cell embryos lack EED and H3K27me3 while Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos have similar levels.

claim: Zygotic Eed expression begins at or slightly before the 4-cell stage.
source: Four-cell embryos displayed a similar pattern to 2-cell embryos, although a subset of Eedfl/- / Eed-/- ~4-cell embryos displayed reduced EED and H3K27me3 levels, consistent with expression of zygotic EED beginning at or slightly before this stage and its failure in Eed-/- embryos (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from IF quantification data showing reduced EED and H3K27me3 in a subset of Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 4-cell embryos (Figure 2C).

claim: At the ~8-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos showed highly variable EED and H3K27me3 levels.
source: At the ~8-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos showed highly variable EED and H3K27me3 levels, suggesting further differentiation of the two genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Eedm-/- ~8-cell embryos displayed higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the corresponding Eedmz-/- embryos.
source: In agreement with increasing zygotic Eed expression, Eedm-/- ~8-cell embryos displayed higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the corresponding Eedmz-/- embryos (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By the ~16-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos were clearly separated into two categories based on EED levels.
source: By the ~16-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos were clearly separated into two categories. One group had statistically lower levels of EED, while the other group was statistically indistinguishable from Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: The likely genotypes of the two groups of ~16-cell Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos are Eed-/- and Eedfl/-, respectively.
source: Therefore, the likely genotypes of the two groups are Eed-/- and Eedfl/-, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential EED levels observed in the two groups of embryos.

claim: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos.
source: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos, but nevertheless harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos.
source: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos, but nevertheless harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Maternally-derived EED starts declining at ~4-cell stage but is still present at the 16-cell stage.
source: Maternally-derived EED starts declining at ~4-cell stage but is still present at the 16-cell stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data plotted across developmental stages (Figure 2E).

claim: Zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage.
source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claim: Zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos.
source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claim: EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein.
source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claim: A subset of X-linked genes was expressed more robustly from the paternal allele relative to the maternal allele in Eedfl/- and Eed-/- female embryos compared to Eedfl/fl embryos.
source: A subset of X-linked genes was expressed more robustly from the paternal allele relative to the maternal allele in Eedfl/- and Eed-/- female embryos compared to Eedfl/fl embryos (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Paternal X-linked gene expression was not significantly higher in Eed-/- blastocysts compared to Eedfl/- or Eedfl/fl female embryos.
source: However, when the allelic expression ratio of all X-linked genes in Figure 3A was averaged, paternal X-linked gene expression was not significantly higher in Eed-/- blastocysts compared to Eedfl/- (p = 0.72) or Eedfl/fl (p = 0.76) female embryos (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: X-linked genes were expressed predominantly from the maternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
source: X-linked genes were expressed predominantly from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The ratio of maternal:paternal X-linked gene expression in Eed-/- female blastocysts was broadly similar to that in Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- embryos.
source: Thus, the ratio of maternal:paternal X-linked gene expression in Eed-/- female blastocysts was broadly similar to that in Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Pyrosequencing did not detect any significant changes in maternal:paternal allelic expression of Xist, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 in hybrid Eed-/- vs. Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- blastocysts.
source: We did not detect any significant changes in maternal:paternal allelic expression in hybrid Eed-/- vs. Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- blastocysts (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
source: Whereas Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
source: Whereas Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Xist RNA coating and Rnf12 expression in female Eed-/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl blastocysts.
source: Xist RNA coating and Rnf12 expression in female Eed-/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl blastocysts (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Both Eedfl/fl and Eed-/- female blastocysts displayed Xist RNA coating of one X-chromosome and Rnf12 expression from the other X-chromosome in a majority of the cells.
source: Both sets of embryos displayed Xist RNA coating of one X-chromosome and Rnf12 expression from the other X-chromosome in a majority of the cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Male Eed-/- or Eed+/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl embryos in their Rnf12 expression patterns.
source: Male Eed-/- or Eed+/- embryos also did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl embryos in their Rnf12 expression patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: By three independent assays – allele-specific RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH – zygotic Eed expression appears to be largely dispensable for the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation.
source: Thus, by three independent assays – allele-specific RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH – zygotic Eed expression appears to be largely dispensable for the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH experiments.

claim: Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited a small percentage of nuclei with H3K27me3 enrichment coinciding with the Xist RNA coat.
source: Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited a small percentage of nuclei with H3K27me3 enrichment coinciding with the Xist RNA coat (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by IF/RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Eedmz-/- blastocysts lacked all overlapping accumulation of H3K27me3 with the Xist RNA coat.
source: Eedmz-/- blastocysts, on the other hand, lacked all such overlapping accumulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by IF/RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H3K27me3 enrichment on the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- blastocysts is likely due to the expression of zygotic Eed in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- embryos.
source: H3K27me3 enrichment on the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- blastocysts is likely due to the expression of zygotic Eed in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- embryos (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos and the EED expression data in Figure 2.

claim: The RNA-Seq data revealed a relative increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
source: Strikingly, the RNA-Seq data revealed a relative increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos (Figure 4B and C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Eedmz-/- embryos appeared to express paternal X-linked genes to a greater degree compared to Eedm-/- embryos.
source: Furthermore, Eedmz-/- embryos appeared to express paternal X-linked genes to a greater degree compared to Eedm-/- embryos (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in average allelic expression between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos did not reach statistical significance (p=0.14).
source: When allelic expression ratios of all X-linked genes in Figure 4B were averaged, however, the difference between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos did not reach statistical significance (p=0.14) (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Paternal X-linked genes significantly increased in expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
source: Whereas paternal X-linked genes significantly increased in expression, maternal X-linked gene expression decreased in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Maternal X-linked gene expression decreased in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
source: Whereas paternal X-linked genes significantly increased in expression, maternal X-linked gene expression decreased in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos was significant when compared to the three other genotypes.
source: The increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos was significant when compared to the three other genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: The decrease in maternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos reached significance only vs. Eedfl/fl embryos and not vs. Eedfl/- and Eed-/- embryos.
source: The decrease in maternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos reached significance only vs. Eedfl/fl embryos and not vs. Eedfl/- and Eed-/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Eedmz-/- embryos displayed a significant increase in paternal X-linked gene expression compared to Eedm-/- embryos (p=0.02).
source: Finally, Eedmz-/- embryos displayed a significant increase in paternal X-linked gene expression compared to Eedm-/- embryos (p=0.02; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3), suggesting that zygotic EED can contribute to the silencing of a subset of X-linked genes in blastocysts.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Zygotic EED can contribute to the silencing of a subset of X-linked genes in blastocysts.
source: Finally, Eedmz-/- embryos displayed a significant increase in paternal X-linked gene expression compared to Eedm-/- embryos (p=0.02; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3), suggesting that zygotic EED can contribute to the silencing of a subset of X-linked genes in blastocysts.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Pyrosequencing showed a significant defect in the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.
source: Pyrosequencing also showed a significant defect in the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos, Xist expression unexpectedly increased from the maternal-X relative to the paternal-X.
source: In Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos, Xist expression unexpectedly increased from the maternal-X relative to the paternal-X.
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The expression of Rnf12 and Atrx increased from the paternal-X relative to the maternal-X in Eedm-/- embryos.
source: Conversely, the expression of Rnf12 and Atrx increased from the paternal-X relative to the maternal-X in Eedm-/- embryos.
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Eedmz-/- embryos, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 displayed nearly equal levels of expression from the maternal and paternal alleles.
source: In Eedmz-/- embryos, in addition to Rnf12 and Atrx, Pgk1 also displayed nearly equal levels of expression from the maternal and paternal alleles.
evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Maternal EED depletion in the oocyte induces Xist from the maternal X-chromosome in the early embryo.
source: The first is that maternal EED depletion in the oocyte induces Xist from the maternal X-chromosome in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-Seq and Pyrosequencing data showing increased maternal Xist expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Maternal PRC2 represses the maternal Xist locus, which is marked by H3K27me3 in the oocyte.
source: This derepression is consistent with maternal PRC2 repressing the maternal Xist locus, which is marked by H3K27me3 in the oocyte [Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the derepression of maternal Xist in Eedm-/- embryos and supported by published ChIP-Seq data showing H3K27me3 at the Xist locus in oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Ectopic Xist induction from the maternal-X results in the silencing of genes on that X-chromosome.
source: Ectopic Xist induction from the maternal-X then results in the silencing of genes on that X-chromosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased maternal X-linked gene expression observed in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Loss of maternal EED induces paternal X-linked genes.
source: The second major suggestion is that loss of maternal EED induces paternal X-linked genes.
evidence: This is supported by the increased paternal X-linked gene expression observed in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Zygotic EED expression contributes to the silencing of a subset of paternal X-linked genes at the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
source: Finally, the data implicate zygotic EED expression in the silencing of a subset of paternal X-linked genes at the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos showing greater paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Most nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female blastocysts displayed a single Xist RNA coat and monoallelic expression of Rnf12.
source: Whereas most nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- females displayed a single Xist RNA coat and monoallelic expression of Rnf12, a subset displayed Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A subset of nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female blastocysts displayed Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes.
source: Whereas most nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- females displayed a single Xist RNA coat and monoallelic expression of Rnf12, a subset displayed Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of nuclei with Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female blastocysts also lacked Rnf12 expression.
source: The majority of these nuclei also lacked Rnf12 expression, suggesting silencing of Rnf12 on both X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eedmz-/- male embryos were present in two distinct morphological classes.
source: Interestingly, Eedmz-/- male embryos were present in two distinct morphological classes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data and morphological observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The first category of Eedmz-/- male embryos was comprised of large, well-developed embryos, which displayed few or no nuclei with Xist RNA coating.
source: The first category was comprised of large, well-developed embryos, which displayed few or no nuclei with Xist RNA coating.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The second category of Eedmz-/- male embryos consisted of underdeveloped embryos, which displayed Xist RNA-coating in much higher proportions (20–60% of nuclei).
source: The second category consisted of underdeveloped embryos, which displayed Xist RNA-coating in much higher proportions (20–60% of nuclei).
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In both sets of Eedmz-/- male embryos, Xist RNA coating was often accompanied by a loss of Rnf12 expression from the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome.
source: In both sets of embryos, Xist RNA coating was often accompanied by a loss of Rnf12 expression from the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome.
evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Xist RNA coating hinders developmental progression by silencing genes on the ectopically Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome.
source: These data suggest that Xist RNA coating hinders developmental progression by silencing genes on the ectopically Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that underdeveloped Eedmz-/- male embryos have higher proportions of Xist RNA-coated nuclei.

claim: Eedmz-/- embryos that adaptively repress Xist may overcome developmental deficiency.
source: Eedmz-/- embryos that adaptively repress Xist may overcome this developmental deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that well-developed Eedmz-/- male embryos have few or no Xist RNA-coated nuclei.

claim: A small number of Eedm-/- female as well as male embryos could live to term.
source: To our surprise, a small number of Eedm-/- female as well as male embryos could live to term (Figure 5C), suggesting that the ectopic Xist RNA expression and coating could be resolved in maternal-null embryos of both sexes.
evidence: This is supported by breeding data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ectopic Xist RNA expression and coating could be resolved in maternal-null embryos of both sexes.
source: To our surprise, a small number of Eedm-/- female as well as male embryos could live to term (Figure 5C), suggesting that the ectopic Xist RNA expression and coating could be resolved in maternal-null embryos of both sexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some Eedm-/- embryos can survive to birth.

claim: Significantly more Eedm-/- females were born compared to males (p=0.02).
source: Interestingly, significantly more females were born compared to males (p=0.02, Two-tailed Student's T-test), suggesting that females can more robustly extinguish ectopic Xist RNA expression compared to males.
evidence: This is supported by breeding data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Females can more robustly extinguish ectopic Xist RNA expression compared to males.
source: Interestingly, significantly more females were born compared to males (p=0.02, Two-tailed Student's T-test), suggesting that females can more robustly extinguish ectopic Xist RNA expression compared to males.
evidence: This is inferred from the sex ratio of live born Eedm-/- animals.

claim: Zygotic EED expression is sufficient to compensate for the absence of maternal EED in a subset of the early embryos.
source: These data further suggest that zygotic EED expression is sufficient to compensate for the absence of maternal EED in a subset of the early embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some Eedm-/- embryos can survive to birth.

claim: Eedmz-/- embryos are expected to be inviable.
source: Eedmz-/- embryos are expected to be inviable, since loss of zygotic Eed expression results in lethality of both female and male embryos (Faust et al., 1995; Shumacher et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on published literature showing that zygotic Eed is essential for embryonic development.

claim: Instead of undergoing imprinted inactivation of the paternal X-chromosome, Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- blastocysts switch to random X-inactivation of either the maternal- or the paternal-X in individual cells.
source: We thus postulated that instead of undergoing imprinted inactivation of the paternal X-chromosome, Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- blastocysts switch to random X-inactivation of either the maternal- or the paternal-X in individual cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the discrepancy between RNA FISH and RNA-Seq/Pyrosequencing data.

claim: X-inactivation mosaicism would explain the silencing of maternal X-linked genes and the induction of paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female embryos detected by RNA-Seq and Pyrosequencing.
source: Such mosaicism would explain the silencing of maternal X-linked genes and the induction of paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female embryos detected by RNA-Seq and Pyrosequencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hypothesis of random X-inactivation in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos.

claim: Allele-specific Xist RNA FISH displayed Xist RNA expression from only the paternal-X in Eedfl/+ female blastocysts.
source: Allele-specific Xist RNA FISH displayed Xist RNA expression from only the paternal-X in Eedfl/+ female blastocysts (Figure 6A), as would be expected from embryos stably undergoing imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In Eedm-/- female blastocysts, some nuclei displayed Xist RNA expression from and coating of the maternal-X, others exhibited Xist RNA expression from and coating of the paternal-X.
source: In Eedm-/- female blastocysts, however, we saw a mosaic distribution of Xist RNA expression and coating. Whereas some Eedm-/- blastocyst nuclei displayed Xist RNA expression from and coating of the maternal-X, others exhibited Xist RNA expression from and coating of the paternal-X.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A subset of nuclei in Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited Xist RNA expression from both the maternal and paternal X-chromosomes.
source: A subset of nuclei in Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited Xist RNA expression from both the maternal and paternal X-chromosomes (Figure 6A), consistent with the non-allele specific Xist RNA FISH data from Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- blastocysts in Figure 5A.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Male Eedm-/- embryos displayed ectopic Xist RNA expression from and coating of their sole maternally-inherited X-chromosome in approximately 50% of nuclei.
source: Male Eedm-/- embryos similarly displayed ectopic Xist RNA expression from and coating of their sole maternally-inherited X-chromosome in approximately 50% of nuclei (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the absence of maternal EED most cells express Xist from both X-chromosomes in early female embryos and from the sole X in early male embryos.
source: Thus, in the absence of maternal EED most cells express Xist from both X-chromosomes in early female embryos and from the sole X in early male embryos.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data in 3-16 cell embryos shown in Figure 7.

claim: By the blastocyst stage, one of the two Xist alleles is stochastically silenced in most female cells and the sole Xist allele is silenced in most male cells.
source: By the blastocyst stage, however, one of the two Xist alleles is stochastically silenced in most female cells and the sole Xist allele is silenced in most male cells.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data comparing early embryos (Figure 7) to blastocysts (Figure 6).

claim: The Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes in female and of the single X in male early preimplantation Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/-mouse embryos resemble the pattern observed in preimplantation human female and male embryos.
source: Intriguingly, the Xist RNA coating of both X-chromosomes in female and of the single X in male early preimplantation Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/-mouse embryos resemble the pattern observed in preimplantation human female and male embryos (Okamoto et al., 2011; Petropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on human embryos.

claim: In early preimplantation human embryos, females display Xist RNA coating of both Xs and males of their sole maternally-inherited X-chromosome.
source: In early preimplantation human embryos, females display Xist RNA coating of both Xs and males of their sole maternally-inherited X-chromosome.
evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: The Xist RNA expression profile in early human embryos may reflect the absence of maternally-derived EED and other core PRC2 proteins in human oocytes.
source: We therefore hypothesized that the Xist RNA expression profile in early human embryos may reflect the absence of maternally-derived EED and other core PRC2 proteins in human oocytes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity between Eedm-/- mouse embryos and human embryos.

claim: Compared to mouse oocytes, human oocytes expressed all four core PRC2 genes (Eed, Ezh2, Ezh1, and Suz12) at negligible levels.
source: Compared to mouse oocytes, human oocytes expressed all four genes at negligible levels (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data from mouse and human oocytes shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The difference in the expression of PRC2 components in oocytes may underlie why early mouse but not human embryos undergo imprinted X-inactivation.
source: This difference in the expression of PRC2 components in oocytes may underlie why early mouse but not human embryos undergo imprinted X-inactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparison of PRC2 expression in mouse and human oocytes and the X-inactivation patterns in the respective embryos.

claim: Upon ablation of Eed in the oocyte and the absence of maternally-derived EED in the embryo, the initiation of imprinted X-inactivation is compromised.
source: Upon ablation of Eed in the oocyte and the absence of maternally-derived EED in the embryo, the initiation of imprinted X-inactivation is compromised (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: PRC2-catalyzed H3K27me3 marks the Xist locus on the maternal X-chromosome during oogenesis.
source: PRC2-catalyzed H3K27me3 marks the Xist locus on the maternal X-chromosome during oogenesis (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on published ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The injection of the H3K27me3 demethylase Kdm6b in the zygote resulted in the derepression of the Xist locus on the maternal X-chromosome in 8–16 cell embryos.
source: In agreement, the injection of the H3K27me3 demethylase Kdm6b in the zygote resulted in the derepression of the Xist locus on the maternal X-chromosome in 8–16 cell embryos (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Female morulas derived from Kdm6b-injected zygotes displayed Xist RNA coating of both the maternal and the paternal X-chromosome in most blastomeres.
source: Female morulas derived from Kdm6b-injected zygotes displayed Xist RNA coating of both the maternal and the paternal X-chromosome in most blastomeres, suggesting inactivation of both Xs in the embryo.
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Nullizygosity of X-linked gene expression due to inactivation of both Xs in females or of the single-X in males is expected to result in cell and embryo lethality.
source: Nullizygosity of X-linked gene expression due to inactivation of both Xs in females or of the single-X in males is expected to result in cell and embryo lethality (Gayen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on published literature and biological knowledge.

claim: By the blastocyst stage most nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female embryos exhibit only one Xist RNA coat.
source: In agreement, our study shows that by the blastocyst stage most nuclei in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female embryos exhibit only one Xist RNA coat.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Instead of Xist RNA coating exclusively of the paternal X-chromosome as in WT embryos, the maternal Eed mutants express Xist RNA from and coat either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome, a hallmark of random X-inactivation.
source: However, instead of Xist RNA coating exclusively of the paternal X-chromosome as in WT embryos, the maternal Eed mutants express Xist RNA from and coat either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome, a hallmark of random X-inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Randomization of X-inactivation in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- females persists later in development in extraembryonic tissues.
source: This randomization persists later in development in extraembryonic tissues (data not shown), which normally maintain imprinted inactivation of the paternal-X.
evidence: This is stated but data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- male blastocysts extinguish ectopic Xist induction.
source: Like Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- females, Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- male blastocysts also extinguish ectopic Xist induction.
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Eedmz-/- female blastocysts displayed a further increase in paternal X-linked gene expression compared to Eedm-/- embryos.
source: In addition to maternal EED, our data argue that zygotically generated EED contributes to imprinted X-inactivation in the early embryo. In comparison to Eedm-/- embryos, Eedmz-/- female blastocysts displayed a further increase in paternal X-linked gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The onset of zygotic EED expression results in the preferential installation of H3K27me3 at the Xist locus on the maternal-X in some cells of early Eedm-/- embryos.
source: One interpretation of these data is that the onset of zygotic EED expression results in the preferential installation of H3K27me3 at the Xist locus on the maternal-X in some cells of early Eedm-/- embryos.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Zygotic EED functions to maintain silencing preferentially of paternal X-linked genes in the early embryo.
source: An alternative possibility is that zygotic EED functions to maintain silencing preferentially of paternal X-linked genes in the early embryo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The differential sensitivity of genes on the maternal vs. paternal X-chromosomes to zygotic EED in Eedm-/- embryos may reflect the different kinetics of inactivation of the two X-chromosomes.
source: The differential sensitivity of genes on the maternal vs. paternal X-chromosomes to zygotic EED in Eedm-/- embryos may reflect the different kinetics of inactivation of the two X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The ectopic induction of Xist and X-linked gene silencing on the maternal-X may occur more slowly compared to that on the paternal-X.
source: The ectopic induction of Xist and X-linked gene silencing on the maternal-X may occur more slowly compared to that on the paternal-X.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Zygotic EED is required to maintain silencing of a discrete set of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation.
source: Our previous work has shown that zygotic EED is in fact required to maintain silencing of a discrete set of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006; Maclary et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, as cited.

claim: The ability of the cells of early Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos to resolve Xist RNA coating of both Xs in females or of the single X in males implies that the early mouse embryo has an X-chromosome counting mechanism.
source: The ability of the cells of early Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos to resolve Xist RNA coating of both Xs in females or of the single X in males implies that the early mouse embryo has an X-chromosome counting mechanism that ensures that a single X-chromosome remain active in females as well as in males, irrespective of its parent of origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos can resolve ectopic Xist expression.

claim: The early mouse embryo has an X-chromosome counting mechanism that ensures that a single X-chromosome remain active in females as well as in males, irrespective of its parent of origin.
source: The ability of the cells of early Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos to resolve Xist RNA coating of both Xs in females or of the single X in males implies that the early mouse embryo has an X-chromosome counting mechanism that ensures that a single X-chromosome remain active in females as well as in males, irrespective of its parent of origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos can resolve ectopic Xist expression.

claim: Such a counting mechanism has previously been proposed by Takagi and colleagues to explain the kinetics of Xist RNA induction in XX and XY androgenetic embryos.
source: Such a counting mechanism has previously been proposed by Takagi and colleagues to explain the kinetics of Xist RNA induction in XX and XY androgenetic embryos, which harbor only paternal X-chromosomes (Okamoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Androgenetic 4 and 8–16 cell embryos initially induce Xist RNA from all Xs, which is resolved at the blastocyst stage.
source: Like in Eedm-/- embryos, androgenetic 4 and 8–16 cell embryos also initially induce Xist RNA from all Xs, which is resolved at the blastocyst stage and results in females displaying a single Xist RNA coat in most nuclei and males exhibiting few or no nuclei with Xist RNA coating (Okamoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Molecular sensing of the X-chromosomal complement in imprinted X-inactivation is suggested by studies of diploid XX parthenogenetic or gynogenetic embryos.
source: Molecular sensing of the X-chromosomal complement in imprinted X-inactivation is also suggested by studies of diploid XX parthenogenetic or gynogenetic embryos, which harbor two maternal X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: In diploid XX parthenogenetic or gynogenetic preimplantation embryos, Xist expression is delayed and appears to occur stochastically from one or the other X-chromosome.
source: In these preimplantation bi-maternal XX embryos, Xist expression is delayed and appears to occur stochastically from one or the other X-chromosome (Kay et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: The extraembryonic tissues of post-implantation XX parthenogenotes display hallmarks of random X-inactivation instead of the imprinted form observed in WT extraembryonic cells.
source: In agreement, the extraembryonic tissues of post-implantation XX parthenogenotes display hallmarks of random X-inactivation instead of the imprinted form observed in WT extraembryonic cells (Rastan et al., 1980).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Imprinted X-inactivation in placental mammals may have arisen from random X-inactivation.
source: Randomization of X-inactivation in extraembryonic cells of mouse embryos with two paternal or maternal X-chromosomes led Takagi and colleagues to suggest that imprinted X-inactivation in placental mammals may have arisen from random X-inactivation (Matsui et al., 2001), a notion that our data from Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos agree with.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by others and supported by the data in this study.

claim: The maternal-X allele of Rnf12 is required to induce Xist from the paternal-X in preimplantation mouse embryos.
source: The maternal-X allele of Rnf12 is required to induce Xist from the paternal-X in preimplantation mouse embryos (Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Upon Xist RNA coating, Rnf12 is rapidly silenced on the paternal X-chromosome.
source: Upon Xist RNA coating, Rnf12 is rapidly silenced on the paternal X-chromosome (Kalantry et al., 2009; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: In Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos, the maternal Rnf12 allele is stringently silenced due to ectopic Xist RNA coating of the maternal-X.
source: In Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos, in addition to the paternal Rnf12 allele, the maternal Rnf12 allele is also stringently silenced due to ectopic Xist RNA coating of the maternal-X.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA FISH data showing loss of Rnf12 expression in cells with Xist RNA coating of both Xs.

claim: The silencing of all Rnf12 alleles in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female and male embryos may lead to the loss of Xist RNA expression from both Xs in females or from the sole X-chromosome in males.
source: Since Rnf12 is required for Xist RNA induction in the preimplantation embryo, the silencing of all Rnf12 alleles in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- female and male embryos may paradoxically lead to the loss of Xist RNA expression from both Xs in females or from the sole X-chromosome in males.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the resolution of ectopic Xist expression.

claim: In females, the transient state of two active-Xs may be followed by random X-inactivation, analogously to how differentiating pluripotent epiblast cells undergo random X-inactivation.
source: In females, this transient state of two active-Xs may then be followed by random X-inactivation, analogously to how differentiating pluripotent epiblast cells undergo random X-inactivation (Gayen et al., 2015; Maclary et al., 2014; Mak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the randomization of X-inactivation in Eedm-/- embryos.

claim: The X-chromosome counting process and randomization of X-inactivation in the early embryo may explain how Eedm-/- embryos can yield live born animals.
source: The X-chromosome counting process and randomization of X-inactivation in the early embryo may explain how Eedm-/- embryos can yield live born animals [this study and (Prokopuk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data and cited literature.

claim: Extraembryonic tissues of Eed maternal-null female post-implantation embryos exhibit random X-inactivation.
source: In the course of preparing this manuscript, a publication reported that extraembryonic tissues of Eed maternal-null female post-implantation embryos exhibit random X-inactivation (Inoue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a published study by another group.

claim: The primary piece of data in the Inoue et al. study supporting the conclusion of random X-inactivation is the expression of maternal and paternal X-linked genes, including Xist, in post-implantation E6.5 female Eedm-/- extraembryonic tissues by allele-specific RNA-Seq.
source: The primary piece of data in the study supporting this conclusion is the expression of maternal and paternal X-linked genes, including Xist, in post-implantation E6.5 female Eedm-/- extraembryonic tissues by allele-specific RNA-Seq.
evidence: This is a description of data from a published study by another group.

claim: The Inoue et al. study did not directly demonstrate when imprinted X-inactivation switches to random X-inactivation and whether loss of zygotic Eed would result in a similar outcome.
source: Although in agreement with our conclusions, the study did not directly demonstrate when imprinted X-inactivation switches to random X-inactivation and whether loss of zygotic Eed would result in a similar outcome.
evidence: This is a critique of the Inoue et al. study.
